opus-5.5.text:
I think the gap is real, but it's not quite where people usually assume it is. A lot of people imagine that the hard part is dexterity: folding a shirt, wiping a counter, loading a dishwasher. Those things are hard, but in some sense we've started to see that if you collect enough data and train a large enough model, you can get a robot to do a pretty impressive job at a specific physical skill. What's much harder is everything around the skill.

A housekeeper isn't just executing a sequence of motions. They walk into a home they've never seen, figure out where things go, notice that something's spilled, decide that the laundry can wait but the stove can't, and recover when the drawer is stuck or the dog knocks something over. That requires generalization, common sense, and the ability to string together long-horizon behavior where mistakes compound. If your robot is 95% reliable on each step and the task has fifty steps, you're basically guaranteed to fail somewhere. So robustness and recovery matter enormously, and you only get those by seeing a huge diversity of situations, including your own failures.

The way I think about it, the path from one to the other isn't a series of hand-engineered extensions. It looks a lot more like what happened in language models: you build a general-purpose foundation that's trained on lots of different robots, tasks, and environments, and then the specialization becomes the easy part. The repeated task in a factory is like a narrow classifier; the housekeeper is like a general-purpose assistant. And I think the key that unlocks the second is getting robots into the real world early, doing useful but imperfect things, so they can keep collecting experience and improving, ideally with some amount of autonomous learning on top of imitation. Once you have that flywheel going, I'm actually fairly optimistic that the gap closes faster than people expect. Not overnight, but on the order of years rather than decades.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a robot performing a specific physical skill with a housekeeper handling varied tasks, decisions, and recovery, conveying a broader scope of delegated responsibility.

r002.rationale: The response compares robots to language models and general-purpose assistants, but does not mention coding assistants progressing toward broader assignments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the way I'd frame it is that the gap is actually not so much about the difficulty of any individual task. If you look at the kinds of things a housekeeper does, folding laundry, loading a dishwasher, wiping down a counter, each of those in isolation is something we can get a robot to do today in a lab, often pretty convincingly. The gap is really about breadth and robustness. The repeated-task robot works because somebody has carefully constrained the world for it. The objects are always the same, the lighting is the same, the position is the same, and if anything deviates, it just fails, and a person comes and resets it. The housekeeper has to work in a world that nobody constrained for them, where every house is different, every shirt is different, and things go wrong constantly in ways you didn't anticipate.

And the thing that I think people sometimes underestimate is that this is fundamentally a data problem, in the same way that it was for language and vision. The reason a language model can handle an enormous range of situations is that it's seen an enormous range of situations. In robotics we historically didn't have that, so we engineered around it, and engineering around it is exactly what gives you the brittle single-task system. So the way I think about closing the gap is, how do you get a foundation model for robots that has the kind of broad prior about the physical world that a language model has about text, so that when it encounters a new kitchen, it's not starting from scratch, it's just adapting something it mostly already knows.

The other piece, which is more subtle, is the long horizon. Doing a task is one thing. Doing a sequence of tasks over an hour, noticing when something went wrong and recovering from it, that's where I think a lot of the real difficulty is, and it's where the reasoning capabilities from language models actually start to matter for robotics. So I'd say the housekeeper is maybe less far away than it looks if you're counting individual skills, and further away than it looks if you're counting how reliably those skills need to compose.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the gap to breadth, robustness, and long-horizon task composition, but does not characterize it as a difference in the scope of responsibility delegated to the robot.

r002.rationale: It compares robotics foundation models to language models, but makes no analogy to coding assistants taking on broader assignments.

astra-6.text:
I think the gap is less about whether the robot can perform any particular motion and more about whether it can handle all the variation that comes with the job. If you have a robot doing a repeated task, you can arrange the environment so that the same behavior works every time. The object is in the same place, the lighting is similar, and somebody intervenes when something goes wrong.

A housekeeper has to deal with an environment that hasn’t been arranged for it. Every house is different. Even in the same house, things move around. And the task itself is underspecified. If I say, “Clean up the kitchen,” you have to infer what belongs where, what should be thrown away, and what you should ask me about before touching.

Then there’s recovery. Suppose you try to pick up a dish and it slips. That shouldn’t mean the whole system stops working. You need to recognize what happened and decide what to do next. Over a long task, even small failure probabilities become a big problem if you can’t recover.

So I would think of this as the difference between engineering a particular behavior and building a system that can draw on broad experience to handle new situations. The repeated task demonstrates that the robot can execute a skill. The housekeeper needs to know when to use that skill, adapt it to the circumstances, and keep making progress when its first attempt doesn’t work.

r001.rationale: It contrasts a robot executing a fixed skill with a housekeeper responsible for handling varied situations, making decisions, and recovering over a long task.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention coding assistants or compare robots’ expanding responsibilities to their broader assignments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the gap is less about the complexity of any individual motion and more about the range of situations the robot has to handle. If you watch somebody clean a house, most of the individual actions are pretty simple. You pick something up, you put it somewhere else, you wipe a surface. We can build robots that do examples of all those things. But that doesn’t mean we can put them together and get a housekeeper.

The housekeeper has to figure out what needs doing, recognize when something unexpected happens, and recover. You try to pick up a shirt and it’s caught on something. You open a drawer and it’s full. You encounter an object you haven’t seen before, and you have to decide where it belongs. A repeated task can be engineered so that those situations almost never arise. In a home, dealing with those situations is the task.

And then there’s a compounding reliability problem. If you succeed 90 percent of the time on a short action, that can look quite impressive in a demonstration. But if you need a hundred actions to accomplish something, and any failure ends the attempt, you’re very unlikely to finish. So you need both much higher reliability and the ability to notice mistakes and correct them.

My view is that getting there requires systems that learn from a very broad range of experience, so they can reuse what they’ve learned across tasks and environments. You don’t want to separately engineer every contingency in every kitchen. You want a robot that has enough general understanding and physical experience to work out what to do in a new one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts a narrowly engineered repeated task with a housekeeper responsible for deciding what needs doing and handling unexpected situations across a home, communicating a broader scope of delegated responsibility.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention coding assistants or compare robots’ expanding responsibilities with broader coding assignments.
